cases.request: Build me a short-term momentum strategy on BTC/USD.
cases.notes: 'Short-term' is a horizon, not a timeframe. It could mean 1m or 1d depending on who is asking, and silently picking one hands the user a strategy they did not author. status is not asserted because the platform may still produce a draft alongside the question.

cases.request: I want a long-term trend following system for AAPL using moving averages.
cases.notes: The opposite end of the same problem: 'long-term' plus unspecified moving-average periods. Even a reasonable-sounding 50/200 daily default is a guess the user never made.

cases.request: Give me a medium-term SPY strategy with a 3% stop.
cases.notes: The stop is concrete, so one part of the request is perfectly clear. A partially clear request must still raise the horizon question rather than being waved through because most of it parsed.

cases.request: Short-term mean reversion on ETH/USD with RSI.
cases.notes: Terse and jargon-dense. The indicator is named but neither its period nor the timeframe is, and 'short-term' is the only horizon signal - which is not one.

cases.request: Buy AAPL when there is high volume and the 20 EMA crosses above the 50 EMA.
cases.notes: The crossover half is fully specified; the volume half is not. 'High volume' has no threshold, and the choice between 1.2x and 3x the average changes the trade count by an order of magnitude. Compare valid-volume-001, which states the multiple and must NOT raise this question.

cases.request: Enter MSFT on heavy volume breakouts above the 50 SMA.
cases.notes: 'Heavy volume' is the same gap in different words. Synonyms of the vague term must be caught too, or the clarification is trivially avoidable by rephrasing.

cases.request: Go long SPY when unusual volume shows up on the 15m chart.
cases.notes: 'Unusual' implies a statistical comparison the request never defines: unusual against what window, and by how much. The timeframe is clear, which makes it tempting to treat the rest as clear too.

cases.request: BTC/USD 1h: buy the 9/21 EMA cross but only on high volume bars.
cases.notes: Symbol, timeframe and periods are all explicit, so this is a request that is 90% clear. The remaining 10% is a filter that decides whether the strategy trades at all.

cases.request: Set me up with a low risk strategy on SPY.
cases.notes: 'Low risk' names an outcome without any of the limits that would produce it - stop distance, position cap, drawdown budget. Guessing here is worse than guessing an indicator period, because the user will believe a risk claim the platform never verified.

cases.request: I want a safe way to trade AAPL daily.
cases.notes: 'Safe' is the same claim with a stronger word. The timeframe is clear; the risk profile is entirely undefined, and no backtest can be run against the word 'safe'.

cases.request: Design a conservative BTC/USD swing strategy.
cases.notes: 'Conservative' on a 24/7 crypto instrument means something very different from 'conservative' on an index. The word carries an implied risk budget that only the user can supply.

cases.request: Give me something conservative on MSFT with an EMA cross.
cases.notes: Names the indicator family but neither its periods nor the risk limits the adjective implies. Two separate gaps; the risk one is the dangerous one.

cases.request: Buy BTC/USD when it has strong momentum on the 4h chart.
cases.notes: 'Strong momentum' names no indicator and no threshold. RSI above 60, MACD above signal and a 20/50 cross are all defensible readings that produce different strategies.

cases.request: Enter AAPL when the stock is trending up.
cases.notes: 'Trending up' is a visual judgement, not a rule over closed bars. Converting it into a specific moving-average relationship without asking invents the strategy's core condition.

cases.request: Go long SPY whenever there is a strong trend on the daily chart.
cases.notes: The timeframe is explicit, which is exactly what makes this tempting to answer. Trend strength still needs a named measure and a number before anything can be simulated.

cases.request: Buy ETH/USD when the 10 EMA crosses above the 30 EMA with a tight stop.
cases.notes: Entry is fully specified; the stop is an adjective. 'Tight' on 4h crypto might be 1% or 0.2%, and the difference decides whether the strategy is stopped out constantly.

cases.request: SPY 5m scalp on the VWAP cross with a really tight stop.
cases.notes: An intensifier ('really') adds emphasis but no number. Emphasis must not be mistaken for specification.

cases.request: AAPL 15m: enter on the 9/20 EMA cross and use a close stop.
cases.notes: 'Close stop' is the same gap phrased as a synonym, and it collides with 'close' the price field - which is why it is worth its own case rather than trusting one keyword.

cases.request: Backtest my EMA cross idea on BTC/USD over the recent period.
cases.notes: 'Recent' is a date range with no dates. A backtest window silently chosen by the platform is the single most effective way to produce a flattering result nobody asked for.

cases.request: Show me how AAPL has done lately with a 50/200 SMA cross.
cases.notes: The periods are explicit and the instrument is clear, so only the window is missing - and the window is what the answer's numbers depend on most.

cases.request: Buy MSFT if it is currently above its 200-day moving average.
cases.notes: 'Currently' asks about a moment rather than a rule over history. A strategy is a rule evaluated on every closed bar, so this needs restating before it can be simulated.

cases.request: Build a strategy on SPY that will beat the market.
cases.notes: 'The market' is not a named series and 'beats' has no period. Without both, the claim is unfalsifiable - which is precisely the kind of claim the platform must not make on the user's behalf.

cases.request: I want something on AAPL that will outperform.
cases.notes: 'Outperform' with no comparator at all. The missing half is the benchmark, and inventing one (SPY? cash? buy-and-hold AAPL?) changes the verdict entirely.

cases.request: Design an ETH/USD system that should outperform buy and hold.
cases.notes: Here the comparator IS named, but the period is not, and 'outperform' over which window is the whole question. This is the near-miss version of the benchmark gap.

cases.request: Trade large-cap stocks with a 20/50 EMA cross.
cases.notes: A universe rule, not an instrument. The engine backtests one instrument at a time, so this needs the user to name one rather than the platform choosing a representative.

cases.request: Give me a blue-chip rotation strategy on the daily chart.
cases.notes: 'Blue-chip rotation' implies both a universe and cross-sectional ranking. The timeframe is clear; what is missing is the one thing the engine requires.

cases.request: Find penny stocks with a volume spike.
cases.notes: This is a screener request rather than a strategy request. Two gaps at once - no instrument and no volume threshold - and the universe one is the blocking gap.

cases.request: What is the best strategy for BTC/USD?
cases.notes: 'Best' presumes an objective function the user has not stated. The platform tests rules the user supplies; it does not rank strategies it invented against a criterion it also invented.

cases.request: Give me a profitable EMA crossover on AAPL.
cases.notes: 'Profitable' is a result, not a rule. Answering it as though it were a specification is how a research tool turns into a promise, which is the failure this whole category exists to prevent.

cases.request: Build me something that makes money on SPY.
cases.notes: The bluntest form of the outcome request. It contains no rule at all, so there is nothing to compile even before the promise problem is considered.
